item.title: The Rainbow Bridge Poem
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Read the full Rainbow Bridge Poem.

The post The Rainbow Bridge Poem appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
Attributed to Edna Clyne-Rekhy

Just this side of heaven is a place called Rainbow Bridge.

When an animal dies that has been especially close to someone here, that pet goes to Rainbow Bridge. There are meadows and hills for all of our special friends so they can run and play together.

There is plenty of food, water and sunshine, and our friends are warm and comfortable.

All the animals who had been ill and old are restored to health and vigor. Those who were hurt or maimed are made whole and strong again, just as we remember them in our dreams of days and times gone by.

The animals are happy and content, except for one small thing; they each miss someone very special to them, who had to be left behind.

They all run and play together, but the day comes when one suddenly stops and looks into the distance. His bright eyes are intent. His eager body quivers. Suddenly he begins to run from the group, flying over the green grass, his legs carrying him faster and faster.

You have been spotted, and when you and your special friend finally meet, you cling together in joyous reunion, never to be parted again. The happy kisses rain upon your face; your hands again caress the beloved head, and you look once more into the trusting eyes of your pet, so long gone from your life but never absent from your heart.

Then you cross Rainbow Bridge together.

Donate in Memory of a Pet Who Touched Your Heart

item.title: New Jersey Ranks 15th in Nation for Protection of Service Dog Handlers
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Learn more about The Seeing Eye's first-of-its-kind State of Access Report card.

The post New Jersey Ranks 15th in Nation for Protection of Service Dog Handlers appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
The Seeing Eye, based in Morristown, recently released the State of Access Report card, a first-of-its-kind study of how well all 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico protect the rights of service dog teams. Each jurisdiction was graded on 5 subjects and ranked from 1 to 52. New Jersey received a C+, just above the national average of C, and ranked 15th in the nation.

“People who are blind deserve to move through the world independently and with confidence, and a Seeing Eye dog is a powerful partner in that goal,” said Karen Leies, President and CEO of The Seeing Eye. “However, the data we collected reveals serious and persistent gaps in protections not only for guide dog handlers, but for all types of service dog teams across the country. This report card is our call to greater public education and action.”

Just 14 jurisdictions across the U.S. earned a B grade or higher, meaning fewer than 1 in 4 service dog handlers live in a state with strong, comprehensive protections. Approximately 30 percent of all ranked jurisdictions (16 of 52) received a D or F, signaling critically weak protection across a large swath of the country

In New Jersey, The Seeing Eye is advocating for legislation that would require education for business owners, their employees, and law enforcement officers, and stricter penalties for discrimination and access denials.

The full report card is now available, and there is a free app for Apple and Android devices called the Seeing Eye Advocacy App that allows users to look up laws in each state and provides information about how someone can file a complaint if they experience discrimination.

Tips for Business Owners

  • Service dogs are welcome everywhere customers are. Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, service dogs must be allowed access to all public areas of an establishment, restaurants, grocery stores, hotels, public transportation, taxis and rideshares.
  • Know the two questions you may ask. It is illegal to require identification or certification for a service dog. If it isn’t obvious why the dog is needed, staff may ask only two questions. 1. Is the animal required because of a disability? 2. What work or task has the animal been trained to perform?
  • Don’t charge extra. It is illegal to require a fee, deposit or surcharge for a service animal.
  • Know when it’s ok to say NO. Public entities may deny access to service animals if the dog is not housebroken or the person working with the dog does not effectively control the dog. Service dogs should always be leashed and on the floor at all times unless a person’s disability requires them to use another means of controlling the dog.
  • Learn more about the rights and responsibilities of handlers and business owners in food establishments, lodging, health care facilities, housing, transportation and more by visiting The Seeing Eyes online advocacy center at seeingeye.org/advocacy.

The post New Jersey Ranks 15th in Nation for Protection of Service Dog Handlers appeared first on The Seeing Eye.

Puppy Club!

The post Full of Paws-abilities: The Luzerne County Puppy Club appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
Over 25 years ago, the small but mighty PawsAbilities Luzerne County club was founded. Current members join in on the fun from Luzerne, Lackawanna and Monroe Counties in Pennsylvania.

“We have five members who work in schools, so our puppies get a ton of practice in schools and visiting classrooms,” said puppy club leader Michelle Sminkey.

One of the highlights of the club each year is its participation in “Read Across America” where students practice their reading skills by reading aloud to Seeing Eye puppies. Club members also frequently enjoy engaging the local community and educating them about guide dogs through presentations to local scout troops, Lions clubs, churches, and colleges.

item.title: July 26 is Disability Independence Day
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Sr. Specialist, Advocacy & Government Relations, Melissa Allman, reflects on the history and future of advocacy efforts.

The post July 26 is Disability Independence Day appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
By: Melissa Allman, Sr. Specialist, Advocacy & Government Relations

We couldn’t let the 36th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act go by without taking another deep dive into The Seeing Eye archives.

On July 26, 1978, 12 years to the day before the ADA was signed into law, Morris Frank wrote a letter of thanks to William Patterson, the CEO of United Airlines. William Patterson was a longtime ally of The Seeing Eye, and Morris Frank thanked him for always allowing him to fly United with his Seeing Eye dogs and for helping to pave the way for people who are blind to have equal access to other airlines and modes of public transportation with their Seeing Eye dogs.

When Morris Frank wrote this letter, he could not have known that both the Air Carrier Access Act and the ADA would be passed in 1986 and 1990 respectively. Life would have been easier for Morris Frank and early guide dog handlers if these laws had been in place, but Morris Frank was known for his determination and for thinking outside the box. He didn’t need laws to be a pioneer.

When advocacy becomes discouraging, let’s remember that we do have laws to protect us because people like Morris Frank and his allies pushed the envelope, educated people who didn’t even know what Seeing Eye dogs were, and laid a foundation for us.

Let’s honor Morris Frank’s legacy by advocating for our rights when giving up would be easier and by channeling our frustration with injustice into meaningful education. We can use Disability Independence Day as an opportunity to build momentum in small ways. Let’s hold space for stories about access barriers and denials, but also share stories with us about triumphs or times where your education efforts paid off.

Do you want to learn about your rights as a guide dog handler, or do you want to educate someone else about this topic? Check out our Seeing Eye Advocacy App, a resource full of guide dog laws and educational materials for the US and Canada.

item.title: Proud to Raise: Lillian & Frances
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
The positive impact being a puppy raiser during college had on Lillian.

The post Proud to Raise: Lillian & Frances appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
For over 25 years, the Puppy Raisers of the University of Delaware (PRoUD) raisers have lived with the Seeing Eye puppies they are raising in approved on-campus housing. The student volunteers bring them to classes, attend bi-monthly meetings, and participate in exposure outings that prepare the puppies for their future jobs as guides. 

Being a part of the puppy raising community on campus made an impact on recent UD graduate, Lillian Weingarten, never expected.

Dear The Seeing Eye, 

Four years ago, I joined the Puppy Raisers of UD not realizing how much The Seeing Eye would end up shaping my college experience. 
 
Since then, I’ve had the privilege of raising Zia, Rae, Addy, and now Frances. Each pup has made such a huge impact on my life and being part of their journey toward becoming Seeing Eye dogs has been one of the most rewarding parts of college for me. 
 
Through PRoUD, I had the opportunity to serve on fundraising committee, as secretary, and ultimately as president. I also helped plan exposure outings and events and got to be part of such an incredible community that cares so deeply about The Seeing Eye’s mission. From puppy classes and late night walks to trips to Philly and DC, these experiences gave me some of my favorite memories and friendships. 
 
I’m so grateful to The Seeing Eye, our area coordinators, puppy sitters, fellow raisers, and everyone who supported me and my pups along the way. I’ll always be thankful for everything these four years, and these four pups, have given me  

–Lillian

Learn more about our volunteer puppy raising community today!

item.title: Four Tips for Global Accessibility Awareness Day
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Four helpful accessibility tips to celebrate Global Accessibility Awareness Day!

The post Four Tips for Global Accessibility Awareness Day appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
Today marks the 15th Global Accessibility Awareness Day, a day dedicated to educating people about digital accessibility. The Seeing Eye works hard every day to ensure that our website, emails, documents, and social media posts are accessible to everyone.

Some actions we take that you too can take are:

  • Add alternative text (or ALT text) to all photos and graphics you use. This short sentence or two provides a written description of an image.
  • Check that the captions on your videos are accurate.
  • Adding audio descriptions allows people who are blind or low vision to enjoy your content too.
  • Ensure all your webpages and graphics have high color contrast.

The DOJ (Department of Justice) also has a great page on web accessibility. Check it out at https://www.ada.gov/resources/web-guidance/

The post Four Tips for Global Accessibility Awareness Day appeared first on The Seeing Eye.

item.title: Forever Friends: The Passaic County Puppy Club
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Learn more about the Passaic County puppy club's origins, members, and outings

The post Forever Friends: The Passaic County Puppy Club appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
From first to long-time puppy raisers, the Passaic County Seeing Eye puppy club is filled with dedicated volunteers who love being a part of the thriving puppy raising community. 

“It can be intimidating raising a puppy, but I’ve never been alone in any part of it,” said first-time raiser Juliana Arrabito. “From the moment I joined, everyone has been so helpful and kind.” 

The Passaic County club was established in the late 80’s by Alexandra Moguillanes, who continues to tag along with her family for outings and club meetings, but has passed the leadership baton to Janet Drashinsky. 

The club meets twice a month in Pompton Lakes alternating between Pompton Lakes Middle School and St. Mary’s Roman Catholic Church. They also host demonstrations at local schools, libraries, and summer camps to help educate the public about The Seeing Eye’s mission. 

“[Our club] is a dedicated family filled with long time raisers and forever friends,” explained Janet. 

Learn more about the volunteer puppy raising program today!

item.title: State of Access Report Card
item.dc:creator: Michelle Barlak
item.description:
Learn more about The Seeing Eye's State of Access Report Card.

The post State of Access Report Card appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
A national report card on service dog handler rights and protections.

The grades are in! Today, we released our State of Access Report Card, which grades and ranks every U.S. state, Washington, D.C. and Puerto Rico on how well they protect the rights of people who work with service dogs to travel independently and live without compromising their freedom.

This first-of-its-kind data-driven ranking is meant to be a resource for everyone with a stake in service dog handler rights. Whether you are a handler navigating your daily life, an advocate pushing for stronger protection, or a lawmaker with the power to close the gap this data reveals, we hope our report presents a clear picture of where your state stands, along with a roadmap for what meaningful progress looks like.

See how your state scored!

The post State of Access Report Card appeared first on The Seeing Eye.

item.title: The Annual Report 2025: Out Now
item.dc:creator: Megan Fischer
item.description:
Learn about The Seeing Eye's Fiscal Year 2025.

The post The Annual Report 2025: Out Now appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
item.content:encoded:
The Seeing Eye Annual Report covers Fiscal Year 2025, beginning October 1, 2024, and ending September 30, 2025.

As of September 30, 2025, The Seeing Eye has created 18,704 Seeing Eye teams since our founding. Over the last five years, The Seeing Eye has created more guide dog teams than any other program in North America.

At the close of our fiscal year, there were 1,437 active Seeing Eye teams living lives of independence and dignity, mainly in the United States and Canada.

The Annual Report features highlights from Fiscal Year 2025, graduate stories, and other special events held throughout the year. Be sure to check out all these stories and more in The Annual Report 2025, available in audio, Word, and PDF formats.

The post The Annual Report 2025: Out Now appeared first on The Seeing Eye.
